extracted.intended_audience: computer scientists and students writing programs/documentation and referees/editors of academic papers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing literate programs, user manuals, and academic papers, plus best practices for refereeing and preparing galley proofs. Targets exposition, code/module organization, typographic conventions, user-oriented manuals, and referee conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid first-person ('I') in exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Don (and others such as Dijkstra) think the use of ‘I’ in exposition is a bad thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer impersonal tone in technical exposition; avoid author-centric phrasing unless purposely stylistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not start sentences with symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: As in the case of maths, don’t start a sentence with a symbol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite sentences that begin with a symbol (e.g., don’t write ‘data assumes that . . .’); start with words to improve readability and avoid parsing ambiguities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be descriptive and precise with variable names
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions could often be more descriptive; e.g., call a variable caps_range instead of just range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose names that convey meaning; avoid vague names. Prefer nouns for data and verbs for procedures (Truth in Naming).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency between documentation and formal program terms
rubrics_metrics.description: The words used in the documentation should match the words used in the formal program—you will only confuse the reader by using two different terms for the same thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure terminology is consistent across prose, module titles, and code to avoid reader confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment variable declarations when declared away from use
rubrics_metrics.description: In WEB you can declare your variables at any point in the program. Don thinks it is always a good idea to add some comment when you do so, even if only a very cursory explanation is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whenever a variable is declared (especially if distant from its use), add at least a brief comment explaining its purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographic conventions for arithmetic and hexadecimal
rubrics_metrics.description: Be warned that typeset asterisks tend to appear higher above the line than typewritten ones... Better to use × for multiplication, and to use a typewriter-style font with body-centered ‘*’ symbols instead of the ‘*’ in normal typographic fonts. Use typewriter type for hexadecimal numbers, but leave decimal numbers in normal type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use × for multiplication in typeset text; present hex constants in typewriter font (e.g., ‘3F’ in typewriter and the decimal equivalent ‘63’ in normal type) to aid visual checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group related routines/modules together for readability
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the program uses a somewhat specialized data structure (the heap) that might be unknown to the readers, the author should keep all the heap routines together in the text so that they can be read as a group while fresh in the reader’s mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize documentation so readers can view related routines consecutively rather than scattering them; WEB allows arbitrary order—use that freedom to group related material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title capitalization: follow headline convention sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: This student capitalized the first letter of every word in titles of modules... This looks rather unnatural—it is better to follow the newspaper-headlines convention by leaving such words entirely in lowercase, and even better to capitalize only the first word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize only the first word of a module title (and proper nouns); avoid title-casing small words like 'and'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place begins/ends inside called modules (consistent block structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: It’s a good idea to develop the habit of putting your begins and ends inside the called modules, not putting them in the calling module... Appalling bugs will occur if we mix the two conventions!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep block delimiters (begin/end) within the module that implements the functionality rather than in the caller, and be consistent throughout the codebase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modularize error handling (separate error-case code)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many people say that about 25% of any piece of software should be devoted to error handling... WEB provides a solution: The procedure can have a single line near the beginning that says 'Check if the data is wrong' and points to another module. Thus the proper focus is maintained: In the main module we have code devoted to handling the normal cases, and elsewhere we have all the error-case instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep main-path code focused on normal operation; factor error detection/recovery into separate modules that can be implemented and documented thoroughly, increasing motivation to do good error handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use italics for variable names in comments
rubrics_metrics.description: It is good practice to use italics for the names of variables when they appear in comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format variable names distinctively in prose (e.g., italics or code font) to distinguish them from ordinary words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Module title parameters should correspond to local parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the variables in the module title correspond to the local parameters in the module itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When naming or titling a module with parameters, ensure the title's variables match the module's parameter names and semantics to aid comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use correct technical terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: According to this student’s comments, his algorithm uses ‘tail recursion’. This is an impressive phrase, helpful in the proper context; but unfortunately that is not the kind of recursion his program uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure technical terms are used accurately; avoid impressive-sounding but incorrect jargon that misleads readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer nouns for data, verbs for procedures (Truth in Naming)
rubrics_metrics.description: Don commented that the student had given a certain variable the name ‘scan’. Since this variable was essentially a place marker, Don thought that a noun would be much better than a verb—‘place’, perhaps. Let the function determine the part of speech; think of it as a kind of Truth in Naming. Verbs are for procedures, not data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Name variables with nouns and procedures with verbs to reflect their roles and improve readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency in personification ('it' vs 'we')
rubrics_metrics.description: This student also showed a bit of inconsistency in the use of ‘it’ and ‘we’ as the personification of his program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a consistent narrative voice when personifying the program (choose 'it' or 'we' and stick to it) to avoid reader confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write user manuals for naive users; avoid jargon and unexplained technical terms
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea was that the user would need no understanding of computers or of writing... A common failing was that terminology that seemed perfectly transparent meant nothing to Don’s wife: 'Menu' and 'Scrolling' for example. Such terms are so familiar to CS people, it never occurs to them that these are actually technical terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume minimal background; define or avoid jargon; use familiar language and examples when addressing naive users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide clear instructions for undo/exit and error recovery in manuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’s wife commented that one thing she always needs to know is 'How do I get out of a mess if I do something wrong?'... This is something manuals almost never explain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include explicit, jargon-free instructions for exiting, undoing, and recovering from mistakes; make escape routes obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive capitalization and scary prompts
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences like 'And now you should ENTER the data' do nothing to help the user relax—the capitals look too much like DANGER SIGNS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from ALL CAPS for prompts or emphasis; prefer calm, conversational phrasing to avoid intimidating users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer online demonstrations or concise interactive help instead of long descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The manual invited the user to type '?' to get an online demonstration, thus sparing a painful description... If a picture is worth a thousand words, an animated demonstration must be worth at least a paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concise interactive demos or help (e.g., '?' command) and use animations/diagrams to replace long textual explanations where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design sensible keyboard conventions and defaults
rubrics_metrics.description: It was far more natural to type OPTION-N (for 'normal') to leave bold mode rather than OPTION-B again; Option-V was 'reverse video'—why wasn't this OPTION-R? Defaults should carry over (default to style used for preceding line).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose mnemonic key bindings (consistent letters), avoid toggles that force paired keystrokes, and use sensible defaults that persist where users expect them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use diagrams/icons and keyboard diagrams to clarify controls
rubrics_metrics.description: There was a good use of a symbol in the text to indicate the control key, and likewise diagrams of the keyboard to explain which keys to use... There was a nice use of icons to describe scrolling up, down, left, or right though.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include simple diagrams, icons, and keyboard illustrations to clarify controls and reduce reliance on verbose descriptions; explicitly state when a control key must be held down vs typed in sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make ambiguous phrasing explicit
rubrics_metrics.description: One obscurity was the advice 'THIS IS VISIBLE HERE BUT NOT HERE'—Don declared that he didn’t know what this was supposed to mean; it would be a lot better to say 'Extra long messages can be seen if you make them move'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace cryptic or elliptical instructions with explicit, user-centered explanations and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use real data/examples rather than cooked sample data
rubrics_metrics.description: Don observed that a program running on a table of 'real data' is a lot more interesting than the same program running on 'random data'... For illustrating an algorithm, it is better to use 'real' data than 'sample data' cooked up solely as an example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrate algorithms and interfaces with authentic datasets or realistic examples to expose real-world issues and make demonstrations more convincing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep diagrams small but allow detailed figures for interested readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagrams are good if they are kept small... Don disagreed that a figure was too detailed, saying the detail was there for those who want to see it, but could easily be ignored by those who don’t.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer compact diagrams for general comprehension, but include or allow access to more detailed figures for readers who need depth; structure figures so detail can be skimmed over.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide complete and accurate bibliographic details
rubrics_metrics.description: The publishers insisted on more details in his bibliography. They wanted to know, for example, exactly where and when a conference had taken place... libraries often nowadays index conferences by city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include full bibliographic metadata (conference location/date, etc.) to aid indexing and future readers; avoid blind copying of incomplete references that propagate errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carefully check galley proofs and resolve typographic/figure-order issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Don went over galley proofs... At one point he was asked to sanction the insertion of a whole new sentence because he had referenced Figure 14 before Figure 13; the extra comment was wrong but fixable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review galley proofs attentively, verify figure references and ordering, and correct any automated or editorial changes that alter meaning or create errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refereeing: originality is the first criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The first criterion should be originality; is the material presented a genuine advance on previous work?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the submission contributes new knowledge or techniques; if not original, consider whether exposition, pedagogy, or compilation merit publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referees should act as teachers and be constructive
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees should try to be teachers... Try to supply constructive criticism... The referee is conventionally regarded as a sort of 'expert witness,' whose task is to tell the editor whether the paper deserves to be published or not. Don urged referees to see their primary responsibility as being to authors and readers, not just to editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer actionable, polite, and educational feedback aimed at improving the paper rather than merely attacking the author; avoid gratuitous nastiness under anonymity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referees should improve technical quality and provide missing references
rubrics_metrics.description: The referee can contribute to the technical quality of a paper by giving references to related work of which the author was apparently unaware, or improving the results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supply missing citations, point out related literature, suggest technical corrections or enhancements, and where appropriate supply proofs or sketches that clarify the contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize content over grammar when content is hopeless, but polish exposition for worthwhile papers
rubrics_metrics.description: If the content of a paper was obviously bad, he would not spend time reviewing the grammar. But in studying a paper that really has something to say, then he would also try to ensure that it was said as well as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate referee effort proportionally: focus on correctness and originality first; for promising work, also help with clarity and exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use structured review questions or checklists to avoid forgotten issues
rubrics_metrics.description: The referees in this case had been asked to answer a specific list of questions about his paper—Don said that this tedious format might at least cause a referee to consider issues he might otherwise have forgotten about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ a checklist or explicit criteria (originality, correctness, references, exposition, limitations) to ensure comprehensive and consistent reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: When recommending rejection, suggest alternative venues
rubrics_metrics.description: When checking the 'Reject' box, the referee was asked to suggest a less prestigious journal that might publish such inferior work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If recommending rejection, provide constructive guidance on alternative journals or venues and explain what would be required for acceptance elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ambiguous titles and wording that can be parsed in multiple ways
rubrics_metrics.description: One referee pointed out that the paper title 'Optimal Font Caching' could mean caching of optimal fonts or the best caching mechanism for fonts... They solved this by changing the title to 'Optimal Prepaging and Font Caching.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose titles and phrasing that are unambiguous; reword to remove syntactic or semantic ambiguity that could mislead readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use code/typewriter font for sample input/output and to illustrate file data
rubrics_metrics.description: The student gave a nice characterization of the input and output of the program, using the typewriter font to illustrate data as it appears in a file.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render sample files, command examples, and code/data in a monospaced/typewriter font to distinguish them from prose and reflect exact bytes/characters.
